Spatial diffusion and periodic evolving of domain in an SIS epidemic model Thanks: The work is partially supported by the NNSF of China (Grant No. 11771381).

Yachun Tong Affiliation:  School of Mathematical Science, Yangzhou University, Yangzhou 225002, China    Zhigui Lin ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: zglin@yzu.edu.cn (Z. Lin). Affiliation:  School of Mathematical Science, Yangzhou University, Yangzhou 225002, China

Abstract. In order to explore the impact of periodically evolving domain on the transmission of disease, we study a SIS reaction-diffusion model with logistic term on a periodically evolving domain. The basic reproduction number ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} is given by the next generation infection operator, and relies on the evolving rate of the periodically evolving domain, diffusion coefficient of infected individuals dId_{I} and size of the space. The monotonicity of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} with respect to dId_{I}, evolving rate ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) and interval length LL are derived, and asymptotic property of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} if dId_{I} or LL is small enough or large enough in one-dimensional space are discussed. ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} as threshold can be used to characterize whether the disease-free equilibrium is stable or not. Our theoretical results and numerical simulations indicate that small evolving rate, small diffusion of infected individuals and small interval length have positive impact on prevention and control of disease .

MSC: primary: 35K57, 92D30; secondary: 35k55.

Keywords: SIS model; Basic reproduction number; logistic term; periodically evolving domain.

1 Introduction

In recent decades, it is generally recognized that spatial diffusion and environmental heterogeneity have an important impact on the spread of many diseases. Therefore, more and more work is devoted to studying the impact of diffusion on disease control and transmission [2, 4, 12, 32]. In order to capture the impact of spatial heterogeneity of environment and movement of individuals on the persistence and extinction of a disease, Allen et al. [2] proposed a frequency-dependent SIS (susceptible-infected-susceptible) epidemic reaction-diffusion system

{St−dS​Δ​S=−β⁡(x)​S​IS+I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,It−dI​Δ​I=β⁡(x)​S​IS+I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}S_{t}-d_{S}\Delta S=-\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}+\gamma(x)I,&\,x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\[5.69054pt] I_{t}-d_{I}\Delta I=\frac{\beta(x)SI}{S+I}-\gamma(x)I,&\,x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{array}\right.

where S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) and I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) represent the numbers of susceptible and infected individuals at location xx and time tt, respectively; β⁡(x)\beta(x) and γ⁡(x)\gamma(x) are positive bounded Ho¨\ddot{o}lder continuous functions on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}, and denote the rates of contact transmission and disease recovery at xx, respectively; dSd_{S} and dId_{I} are positive constants that denote the diffusion coefficient of susceptible and infected individuals, respectively. Based on the basic reproduction number ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0}, the authors characterised the risk of region. For high domain (ℛ0>1{\mathcal{R}}_{0}>1), the DFE (disease-free equilibrium) is always unstable and there exists a unique EE (endemic equilibrium); in the low risk domain (ℛ0<1{\mathcal{R}}_{0}<1), the DFE is stable if and only if infected individuals have mobility above a threshold value. For some special cases, Peng and Liu [24] proved that unique EE is globally stable, which was conjecture proposed by Allen, et al in [2]. Further results that the effect of individual movement (large or small) on the existence and disappearance of disease were obtained in [23]. Moreover, [25] discussed problem (1) with β\beta and γ\gamma being functions of spatiotemporal variables and temporally periodic, and discovered that spatial heterogeneity and temporal periodicity can enhance the persistence of the disease. More work on system (1) can be found in the literature [14, 12, 13, 18, 39].

Recently, Li, et al [21] considered the following SIS epidemic with logistic source

{St−dS​Δ​S=a⁡(x)​S−b⁡(x)​S2−β⁡(x)​f​(S,I)​I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,It−dI​Δ​I=β⁡(x)​f​(S,I)​I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂S∂ν=∂I∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}S_{t}-d_{S}\Delta S=a(x)S-b(x)S^{2}-\beta(x)f(S,I)I+\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ I_{t}-d_{I}\Delta I=\beta(x)f(S,I)I-\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ \frac{\partial S}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial I}{\partial\nu}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),\ I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where f⁡(S,I)=SS+If(S,I)=\frac{S}{S+I}, β⁡(x)\beta(x), γ⁡(x)\gamma(x), a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x) are positive Hölder continuous functions on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. The nonlinear term a⁡(x)​S−b⁡(x)​S2a(x)S-b(x)S^{2} denotes that the susceptible population is subject to logistic growth. They studied the stability of DFE and EE, and presented the asymptotic profiles of EE as the motility of susceptible or infected individuals is small or large.

It is not difficult to find that all of the above SIS epidemic models are considered in fixed domain, that is, the domain is independent of time tt. In fact, in the natural world, biological habitats usually change over the time. Mathematically, the free boundary can be used to describe the domain change induced by the movement of species. Therefore, the free boundary problem is widely studied in many fields, for example, wound healing [8], the spread of invasive species [15, 17, 35, 36], the transmission of infected disease [6, 7, 16, 20], and so on. However, the free boundary is unknown. On the other hand, the evolving domain is known, such as the change of lake depth due to the alternation of seasons [38], and the spread of mosquito borne diseases due to climate [5]. Owing to the turnover of the four seasons, the evolving of domain is usually periodic. In recent years, some scholars have studied mathematical models on a periodically evolving domain, for example, an SIS epidemic model [28], a mutualistic model [1], an Aedes aegypti mosquito model [40], a dengue fever model [41], and so on. In this paper, we consider the following problem

{St−dS​Δ​S=a⁡(x)​S−b⁡(x)​S2−β⁡(x)​f​(S,I)​I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,It−dI​Δ​I=β⁡(x)​f​(S,I)​I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂S∂ν=∂I∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}S_{t}-d_{S}\Delta S=a(x)S-b(x)S^{2}-\beta(x)f(S,I)I+\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ I_{t}-d_{I}\Delta I=\beta(x)f(S,I)I-\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ \frac{\partial S}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial I}{\partial\nu}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),\ I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega\end{array}\right. (1.4)

on a periodically evolving domain.

As in [9, 31], let Ω⁡(t)⊂𝐑n​(n≥1)\Omega(t)\subset\mathbf{R}^{n}(n\geq 1) be a simply connected bounded shifting domain at time t≥0t\geq 0 with its evolving boundary ∂Ω⁡(t)\partial\Omega(t), and then S¯​(x​(t),t)\bar{S}(x(t),t) and I¯​(x​(t),t)\bar{I}(x(t),t) are the densities of susceptible and infected species at position x⁡(t)x(t) and time t≥0t\geq 0. We can establish the evolution equation on a evolving domain by conservation of mass and Reynolds transport theorem [30]. For any point

x⁡(t)=(x1​(t),x2​(t),…,xn​(t))∈Ω⁡(t).x(t)=(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t))\in\Omega(t).

The evolution of the domain produces a velocity of flow 𝐚=x˙​(t)\mathbf{a}=\dot{x}(t). By Reynolds transport theorem [30], we have

∂S¯∂t+∇S¯⋅𝐚+S¯(∇⋅𝐚)=dSΔS¯+f1(S¯,I¯,t)inΩ(t),∂I¯∂t+∇I¯⋅𝐚+I¯(∇⋅𝐚)=dIΔI¯+f2(S¯,I¯,t)inΩ(t),\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lll}\frac{\partial\bar{S}}{\partial t}+\nabla\bar{S}\cdot\mathbf{a}+\bar{S}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{a})=d_{S}\Delta\bar{S}+f_{1}(\bar{S},\bar{I},t)\ \;\textrm{in}\ \Omega(t),\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial\bar{I}}{\partial t}+\nabla\bar{I}\cdot\mathbf{a}+\bar{I}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{a})=d_{I}\Delta\bar{I}+f_{2}(\bar{S},\bar{I},t)\ \;\textrm{in}\ \Omega(t),\\[5.69054pt] \end{array}

where

f1​(S¯,I¯,t)=a⁡(x)​S¯−b⁡(x)​S¯2−β⁡(x)​f​(S¯,I¯)​I¯+γ⁡(x)​I¯,f2​(S¯,I¯,t)=β⁡(x)​f​(S¯,I¯)​I¯−γ⁡(x)​I¯,f_{1}(\bar{S},\bar{I},t)=a(x)\bar{S}-b(x)\bar{S}^{2}-\beta(x)f(\bar{S},\bar{I})\bar{I}+\gamma(x)\bar{I},\;f_{2}(\bar{S},\bar{I},t)=\beta(x)f(\bar{S},\bar{I})\bar{I}-\gamma(x)\bar{I},

∇S¯⋅𝐚\nabla\bar{S}\cdot\mathbf{a} and ∇I¯⋅𝐚\nabla\bar{I}\cdot\mathbf{a} are called advection terms generated by the evolving domain while (∇⋅𝐚)​S¯(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{a})\bar{S} and (∇⋅𝐚)​I¯(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{a})\bar{I} are called dilution terms caused by the change of element volume and local volume due to local growth and flow movement [10, 11]. In order to deal with the convection term and dilution term caused by regional evolution in equation (1), we use Lagrangian transformations to change equations (1). Let y1,y2,…,yny_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n} be fixed cartesian coordinates in a fixed domain Ω⁡(0)\Omega(0) such that

x1​(t)=x^1​(y1,y2,…,yn,t),x_{1}(t)=\hat{x}_{1}(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n},t),
x2​(t)=x^2​(y1,y2,…,yn,t),x_{2}(t)=\hat{x}_{2}(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n},t),
…\dots
xn​(t)=x^n​(y1,y2,…,yn,t).x_{n}(t)=\hat{x}_{n}(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n},t).

In this transformation, (S¯,I¯)(\bar{S},\bar{I}) is then mapped into the new vector (S,I)(S,I) defined as

S¯​(x1​(t),x2​(t),…,xn​(t),t)=S⁡(y1,y2,…,yn,t),I¯​(x1​(t),x2​(t),…,xn​(t),t)=I⁡(y1,y2,…,yn,t).\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lll}\bar{S}(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t),t)=S(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n},t),\\[5.69054pt] \bar{I}(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t),t)=I(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n},t).\end{array}

Now equations (1) is translated into another form which are defined on the fixed domain Ω⁡(0)\Omega(0) with respect to y=(y1,y2,…,yn)y=(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}), but the new equations are very complicated for arbitrary domain evolution. To further simplify equations (1), we all suppose that domain evolution is uniform and isotropic. In other words, the evolution of the domain occurs in the same proportion in all directions as time increases. From a mathematical point of view, x⁡(t)=(x1​(t),x2​(t),…,xn​(t))x(t)=(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t)) can be described as:

(x1​(t),x2​(t),…,xn​(t))=ρ⁡(t)​(y1,y2,…,yn),\displaystyle(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t))=\rho(t)(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}), y∈Ω⁡(0),\displaystyle y\in\Omega(0), (1.11)

where the positive continuous function ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) is called evolving rate subject to ρ⁡(0)=1\rho(0)=1. The domain is periodically evolving if ρ⁡(t)=ρ⁡(t+T)\rho(t)=\rho(t+T) for some T>0T>0 [19, 29]. The domain is called growing one If ρ˙​(t)≥0\dot{\rho}(t)\geq 0 [30, 31], and when ρ˙​(t)≤0\dot{\rho}(t)\leq 0, the domain is shrinking [37]. Using (1.11) yields

St=S¯t+∇S¯⋅𝐚,It=I¯t+∇I¯⋅𝐚,\displaystyle S_{t}=\bar{S}_{t}+\nabla\bar{S}\cdot\mathbf{a},\quad I_{t}=\bar{I}_{t}+\nabla\bar{I}\cdot\mathbf{a},
𝐚=x˙​(t)=ρ˙​(t)​(y1,y2,…,yn)=ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​(x1,x2,…,xn),\displaystyle\mathbf{a}=\dot{x}(t)=\dot{\rho}(t)(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})=\frac{\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}),
∇⋅𝐚=n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t),Δ​S¯=1ρ2​(t)​Δ​S,Δ​I¯=1ρ2​(t)​Δ​I.\displaystyle\nabla\cdot\mathbf{a}=\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)},\quad\Delta\bar{S}=\frac{1}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta S,\quad\Delta\bar{I}=\frac{1}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta I.

Then (1) becomes

{St=dSρ2​(t)​Δ​S−n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​S+f1​(S,I,t),y∈Ω(0),t>0,It=dIρ2​(t)​Δ​I−n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​I+f2​(S,I,t),y∈Ω(0),t>0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}S_{t}=\displaystyle\frac{d_{S}}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta S-\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}S+f_{1}(S,I,t),&y\in\Omega(0),\,\ t>0,\\[8.53581pt] I_{t}=\displaystyle\frac{d_{I}}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta I-\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}I+f_{2}(S,I,t),&y\in\Omega(0),\,\ t>0.\end{array}\right.

Now we transform the SIS epidemic model on a periodically evolving domain Ω⁡(t)\Omega(t) into the following problem on a fixed domain Ω⁡(0)\Omega(0):

{St−dSρ2​(t)​Δ​S=a⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​S−b⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​S2−β⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​f​(S,I)​I+γ⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​I−n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​S,y∈Ω(0),t>0,It−dIρ2​(t)​Δ​I=β⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​f​(S,I)​I−γ⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​I−n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​I,y∈Ω(0),t>0,∂S∂ν=∂I∂ν=0,y∈∂Ω(0),t>0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llllll}S_{t}-\frac{d_{S}}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta S=a(\rho(t)y)S-b(\rho(t)y)S^{2}-\beta(\rho(t)y)f(S,I)I&\\ \hskip 18.49988pt\hskip 18.49988pt\hskip 18.49988pt+\gamma(\rho(t)y)I-\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}S,&y\in\Omega(0),\;t>0,\\[5.69054pt] I_{t}-\frac{d_{I}}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta I=\beta(\rho(t)y)f(S,I)I-\gamma(\rho(t)y)I-\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}I,&y\in\Omega(0),\;t>0,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial S}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial I}{\partial\nu}=0,&y\in\partial\Omega(0),\;t>0,\end{array}\right.

with the initial condition

S⁡(y,0)=S0​(y)>0,I⁡(y,0)=I0​(y)≥0,I0​(y)≢0,y∈Ω⁡(0)¯.S(y,0)=S_{0}(y)>0,\,I(y,0)=I_{0}(y)\geq 0,\ I_{0}(y)\not\equiv 0,\ y\in\overline{\Omega(0)}. (1.20)

For later application, we also consider problem (1) with the periodic condition

S⁡(y,0)=S⁡(y,T),I⁡(y,0)=I⁡(y,T),y∈Ω⁡(0)¯,S(y,0)=S(y,T),\,I(y,0)=I(y,T),\;\ y\in\overline{\Omega(0)}, (1.21)

where f⁡(S,I)=SS+If(S,I)=\frac{S}{S+I} is monotonically decreasing with respect to II and increasing with respect to SS and limI→0f⁡(S,I)=1\lim\limits_{I\rightarrow 0}f(S,I)=1.

The remainder of the article is organized as below. Section 2 is devoted to the existence and uniqueness of DFE, and Section 3 gives the definition of basic reproduction number and its influence on the stability of DFE. Section 4 is concerned with the limiting behaviors of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} with respect to dId_{I} and LL, and monotonicity of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} with respect to dId_{I}, LL and ρ⁡(t)\rho(t). In the last section, we explain our theoretical results by the numerical simulations.

2 The existence and uniqueness of DFE

In this section, We focus on the existence and uniqueness of the disease-free equilibrium (S∗​(y,t),0)(S^{*}(y,t),0), where (S∗​(y,t),0)(S^{*}(y,t),0) satisfies

{St−dSρ2​(t)​Δ​S=a⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​S−b⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​S2−n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​S,y∈Ω(0),0<t≤T,∂S∂ν=0,y∈∂Ω(0),0<t<T,S⁡(y,0)=S⁡(y,T),y∈Ω⁡(0)¯.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}S_{t}-\frac{d_{S}}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta S=a(\rho(t)y)S-b(\rho(t)y)S^{2}-\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}S,&\ y\in\Omega(0),0<t\leq T,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial S}{\partial\nu}=0,&\ y\in\partial\Omega(0),0<t<T,\\[5.69054pt] S(y,0)=S(y,T),&\ y\in\overline{\Omega(0)}.\end{array}\right.

For existence of the nontrivial solution, we consider the following T-periodic parabolic eigenvalue problem

{ψt−dSρ2​(t)​Δ​ψ=a⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)​ψ−n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)​ψ+λ​ψ,y∈Ω(0),0<t≤T,∂ψ⁡(y,t)∂ν=0,y∈∂Ω(0),0<t<T,ψ⁡(y,0)=ψ⁡(y,T),y∈Ω⁡(0)¯.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\psi_{t}-\frac{d_{S}}{\rho^{2}(t)}\Delta\psi=a(\rho(t)y)\psi-\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}\psi+\lambda\psi,&\ y\in\Omega(0),0<t\leq T,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial\psi(y,t)}{\partial\nu}=0,&\ y\in\partial\Omega(0),0<t<T,\\[5.69054pt] \psi(y,0)=\psi(y,T),&\ y\in\overline{\Omega(0)}.\end{array}\right.

3 Threshold dynamics in terms of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0}

In this section, we first define the basic reproduction number ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0}, and then we study threshold dynamics in terms of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} for problem (1)-(1.20). In general, the basic reproductive number is used to describe the transmission mechanism of the diseases. Biologically, the basic reproduction number ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} is calculated by the next generation matrix method [32] for epidemic models described by spatially-independent systems, or calculated by the next infection operator [34] for models described by spatially-dependent systems.

First, linearizing problem (1) at the disease-free equilibrium (S∗​(y,t),0)(S^{*}(y,t),0) gives

{Ut−D⁡(t)​Δ​U=A⁡(t)​U−B⁡(t)​U,y∈Ω(0),t>0,∂F⁡(y,t)∂ν=0,y∈∂Ω(0),t>0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}U_{t}-D(t)\Delta U=A(t)U-B(t)U,&y\in\Omega(0),t>0,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial F(y,t)}{\partial\nu}=0,&y\in\partial\Omega(0),t>0,\end{array}\right.

with the same periodic condition (1.21), where

B⁡(t)=(n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)+2​b​(ρ⁡(t)​y)​S∗​(ρ⁡(t)​y)β⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)0γ⁡(ρ⁡(t)​y)+n​ρ˙​(t)ρ⁡(t)).B(t)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}+2b(\rho(t)y)S^{*}(\rho(t)y)&\beta(\rho(t)y)\\ 0&\gamma(\rho(t)y)+\frac{n\dot{\rho}(t)}{\rho(t)}\\ \end{array}\right).

Let V⁡(t,s)V(t,s) be the evolution operator of the problem

{wt−D⁡(t)​Δ​w=−B⁡(t)​w,y∈Ω(0),t>0,∂w⁡(y,t)∂ν=0,y∈∂Ω(0),t>0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}w_{t}-D(t)\Delta w=-B(t)w,&y\in\Omega(0),\;t>0,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\partial w(y,t)}{\partial\nu}=0,&y\in\partial\Omega(0),\;t>0.\end{array}\right.

By the standard theory of evolution operators, there exist positive constants KK and c0c_{0} such that

∥V(t,s)∥≤Ke−c0​(t−s),∀t≥s,t,s∈R.\|V(t,s)\|\leq Ke^{-c_{0}(t-s)},\ \ \ \forall t\geq s,\,t,s\in R.

The ordered Banach space CTC_{T} is made up of all T−T- periodic and continuous function from RR to C​(Ω¯​(0),R)C(\overline{\Omega}(0),R), which is equipped with the maximum norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and the positive cone CT+:={ξ∈CT:ξ(t)y≥0,∀t∈R,y∈Ω¯(0)}C_{T}^{+}:=\{\xi\in C_{T}:\xi(t)y\geq 0,\forall\ t\in R,y\in\overline{\Omega}(0)\}. Set ξ⁡(y,t):=ξ⁡(t)​y\xi(y,t):=\xi(t)y for any given ξ∈CT\xi\in C_{T}. The evolution of disease-infected domain is an interesting subject and plays an important role in the study of infectious disease. In order to explore the influence of the periodic evolution in domain on the prevention and control of the infectious disease, we study the SIS reaction-diffusion model with logistic term on a periodically evolving domain.

The purpose of this paper is to analyze the effects of diffusion coefficient of infected individuals dId_{I}, interval length LL and evolving rate ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) on ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0}, and ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} as threshold can be used to characterize stability of the disease-free equilibrium. Firstly, the basic reproduction number ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} is given by the next generation infection operator and relies on the average value of domain evolution rate ρ⁡(t)\rho(t), see the formula (4.61). We then discuss the monotonicity of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} with respect to diffusion coefficient dId_{I} and interval length LL (see Theorem 4.2), and limiting behavior of ℛ0{\mathcal{R}}_{0} if dId_{I} or LL is sufficiently small or sufficiently large in one-dimensional space, see Theorems 4.3 and 4.4. We find that when ℛ0<1{\mathcal{R}}_{0}<1, the disease-free equilibrium (S∗​(y,t),0)(S^{*}(y,t),0) is globally asymptotically stable for system (1)-(1.20), that is to say, the epidemic eventually disappeared; if ℛ0>1{\mathcal{R}}_{0}>1, the disease-free equilibrium (S∗​(y,t),0)(S^{*}(y,t),0) is unstable, in other words, the epidemic persists uniformly, see Theorem 3.2.

In addition, our numerical simulations explain that large evolution rate is unfavorable to control of infectious disease (see Figs. 1 and 2) and small evolution rate is benefit to control of infectious disease (see Figs. 3 and 4). Meanwhile, small diffusion coefficient of infected individuals dId_{I} has a positive effect on the presence of infectious disease (see Figs. 2 and 5). Besides, small habitats facilitate the control of infectious diseases (see Figs. 6 and 7), which is consistent with our understanding.
